name: Cottle maneuver

lead: The Cottle maneuver is a bedside test in which a clinician gently draws the cheek outward to open the nasal valve while the patient breathes. If breathing improves, it suggests internal nasal valve compromise as a cause of obstruction.

For appearance, it matters in rhinoplasty planning: surgeons look for valve weakness so that reshaping the nose does not worsen, and can improve, airflow. Reviews list a positive Cottle maneuver as a risk factor for middle-vault problems after rhinoplasty.[2]

paras: It is done in a clinic by a surgeon or ENT as part of a nasal exam, alongside endoscopy and symptom questionnaires; a modified version uses an instrument or cotton-tip support inside the nose.[4] Treatment, when indicated, may involve spreader or other grafts.[2]
The test itself is low-risk and brief. A 2025 review says such maneuvers are inconsistently used and, alone, are not robust enough to drive surgical decisions.[3]

angle.text: The Cottle maneuver helps surgeons find valve weakness before nose reshaping. That lets them plan grafts so the aesthetic change and airflow are addressed together.

lead: The Cottle maneuver is a physical-examination test for nasal obstruction: the clinician pulls the cheek sideways to widen the nasal valve, and relief of obstruction suggests internal valve compromise. Diagnostic algorithms list the Cottle and modified Cottle maneuvers as key examination components alongside history, endoscopy and quality-of-life questionnaires.[1]

Its link to appearance is surgical planning. Surgeons assessing patients for rhinoplasty look for nasal valve weakness; a positive Cottle maneuver is among risk factors for middle-vault problems that spreader grafts help prevent or repair.[2] Functional and aesthetic middle-vault problems are common reasons for revision rhinoplasty.[2]
Reviews note the test is widely used but inconsistently graded, and a 2025 paper proposes a standardised nasal exam combining grading systems and maneuvers.[3][4]
infobox: ENT or facial plastic surgery clinic

paras: Nasal obstruction is often multifactorial, and valve compromise may be static or dynamic; successful diagnosis rests on history and physical examination.[4] Septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy and valve compromise are among the most common causes seen by facial plastic surgeons.[3]

Risk factors for middle-vault problems include short nasal bones, weak upper lateral cartilages, thin skin, prior surgery and a positive Cottle maneuver; spreader grafts are the workhorse repair.[2] Other reviews discuss middle-vault management and septal extension grafts for alar collapse.[5][6]

A 2025 review states that the maneuver and similar tools, used in isolation, are not robust enough to influence surgical decision-making and proposes standardised exam protocols.[3] A 2024 paper examines objective parameters of internal valve compromise beyond the angle.[7]

Studies include trials of electric stimulation and biofeedback for valve collapse and a study using the modified Cottle test in functional rhinoplasty (this last paper is marked as retracted).[8][9][10]
